analysis.one_liner: Lets the government negotiate lower Medicare prescription drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare drug benefit included a "noninterference" rule that bars the federal government from negotiating drug prices on behalf of Medicare. This bill would delete that rule and let the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate with drug manufacturers, the same way the Department of Veterans Affairs and other big government buyers do. It would also require quarterly reports to Congress comparing the negotiated prices to what uninsured people pay at retail pharmacies.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who pay a share of drug costs, would benefit if the government could negotiate lower prices for the drugs covered under Part D. Taxpayers would benefit too, since Medicare picks up most of the bill for the drug benefit. The bill took effect as if it had been part of the 2003 law, so savings would apply to the program as it exists.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'noninterference' clause added by the 2003 Medicare drug law, which currently prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering with negotiations between drug makers and the private plans and pharmacies that administer the benefit.

Grants the Secretary authority similar to that of other federal agencies that buy prescription drugs in bulk — such as the VA — to negotiate contracts with manufacturers of covered Part D drugs, with the stated goal of ensuring beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price.

Requires quarterly reports to Congress starting in 2007 comparing negotiated Medicare drug prices with the average retail price an uninsured person would pay for the same drug, creating public accountability for whether negotiation is actually producing savings.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, in the form of lower prices on the largest prescription drug market in the country. The private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that run Part D plans could also see their margins squeezed if the government negotiates directly.

drawbacks.text: Critics argued at the time that direct government negotiation amounts to price controls that could reduce pharmaceutical companies' revenues and, over time, their investment in developing new drugs — a tradeoff the bill does not address.

The bill is a single sentence of authority with no enforcement mechanism: it empowers the Secretary to negotiate but does not require any particular outcome, so its real-world savings would depend entirely on how future administrations used the power.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large — Medicare is the nation's biggest drug buyer, and the 2003 law deliberately handcuffed the government from using that leverage, while other federal buyers like the VA negotiate substantial discounts. The cost is uncertain: some reduction in drug-industry revenue and possibly slower development of new drugs, and the bill's open-ended "similar authority" language leaves the actual savings undefined. On balance this was a straightforward consumer-protection measure aimed at lowering out-of-pocket drug costs for seniors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no vote, no action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Arlen Specter introduced the bill on April 15, 2005.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which had jurisdiction over Medicare.
No cosponsors ever signed on, and the committee took no further action; the bill died there when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
This was one of many bills in the 109th Congress to repeal the Part D 'noninterference' clause; none advanced, and the ban on government price negotiation remained in place throughout the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off, because the government's hands stayed tied on Medicare drug prices and no competing bill to authorize negotiation became law during this Congress. The private insurers and middlemen who administer Part D also kept the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers and Part D middlemen

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to authorize Medicare drug price negotiation; no colleague joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; it died there.

against.name: Sen. Charles Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair, never brought the bill up for committee action during the two years it sat in his panel.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed allowing the government to negotiate Medicare drug prices, defending the noninterference clause obtained in the 2003 Medicare law.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and an inactive committee — there was no floor fight to divide along party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed their prices in Medicare — the nation's largest drug market — to direct government negotiation, which the 2003 law deliberately barred. Their interest in keeping the noninterference clause ran directly against seniors' drug costs.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The private plans and middlemen that administer Part D currently handle drug-price bargaining; direct federal negotiation could squeeze their role and margins, though the bill leaves the private-plan structure intact.
